title: Eat, my coat
hook: turned away in rags, welcomed in a fur coat, he spoons the soup into his sleeve

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking under the lamp: Nasruddin searching the street for a key he lost inside. Your line was search where you lost it. Where did you take a step toward the real place? Day thirty-seven.
screen: `LOOKING UNDER THE LAMP — SEARCH WHERE YOU LOST IT.`

segments.voice: Think about how you walk into a nice restaurant in sweatpants, versus how you walk in dressed up. How the host looks at you. Where they seat you. How fast the water arrives. Most of us have been on both sides of that look, and most of us have given it too, without meaning to. Nasruddin, the wise fool of week six, got that look once, at a banquet in his own town. And his answer has become a proverb in Turkish, said to this day whenever someone is treated by their clothes and not by who they are.
screen: `SWEATPANTS, OR DRESSED UP?` → `THE LOOK AT THE DOOR.` → `A BANQUET IN HIS OWN TOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's how the story usually goes. There's a feast, and Nasruddin is invited. He comes straight from work in his everyday clothes, worn and dusty. Nobody greets him. Nobody finds him a seat. The dishes go around and somehow skip him. So he slips out, goes home, and puts on his finest clothes: a big, beautiful fur coat. He walks back in, and everything changes. The host rushes over. Welcome, welcome! He's seated near the top of the table. The best soup is set in front of him. And Nasruddin takes the sleeve of his fur coat, dips it into the bowl, and says: eat, my coat, eat! The guests stare. Mulla, what are you doing? And he says: well, it was the coat you welcomed. It seems only fair the coat should eat. In Turkish, eat, my coat, eat, is a saying people still use, a whole sermon in three words. The old traditions knew this problem well. In Nasruddin's own Muslim world, a well-known saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, teaches that God does not look at your appearance or your wealth, but at your heart and your deeds. And a letter in the New Testament, from James, describes almost the same scene: a rich man in fine clothes is shown to the best seat, and a poor man in shabby clothes is told to stand at the back. Different homes, same banquet. The coat gets the soup, and the person goes hungry. Nasruddin doesn't lecture anyone. He just feeds the coat, and lets the whole room see what they've been doing.
screen: `WORN CLOTHES: NO SEAT.` · `A FUR COAT: THE BEST SOUP.` · `EAT, MY COAT, EAT!` · `NOT APPEARANCE, BUT THE HEART.` · then, large: `FEED THE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then, honestly and without beating yourself up, think back over the last few days. Was there someone you treated a little better because of how they looked, how they dressed, what they drove? Or someone you treated a little worse? The cashier, the new coworker, the person asking for change. Just notice. Then picture that person without the coat. Just a person, hungry for the same things you are. The bell holds the time.
Eat. Nasruddin's words to his fur coat: eat, my coat, eat, because the coat was welcomed, and the man was not.
Your line: feed the person. Today, catch one moment when clothes or looks shape how you treat someone, and treat the person instead. Day thirty-seven.

howItsDone: In Turkey the saying "eat, my coat, eat" is still used to call out treatment based on appearances; many traditions teach hospitality that welcomes every guest the same, such as the Sikh langar and the Muslim and Jewish duty to honor the guest.

original.note: Turkish: eat, my fur coat, eat. Nasreddin Hoca's line, still used as a saying about being judged by appearances.

trapdoor: what you thought: a silly story about a man feeding soup to his coat.
what it means: we welcome the coat and forget to feed the person inside it.
what a scholar hears: kürk is a fur coat; the tale is among the best known in the Turkish Nasreddin Hoca tradition, with Persian and Arabic variants.
